title: Direct inguinal operative anatomy
fairness: The keyed transversalis fascia is defensible for the described direct posterior-wall defect. No convincing medical-knowledge-free wording or length cue was found.

Too easy for PGY-2/3: posterior-wall anatomy is directly requested after the wall and vessel relationship have already been supplied. Naming the hernia and naming its layer are a recall chain, not two consequential inferences.
Importance: core operative anatomy and broadly relevant to general-surgery training; the current layer-identification task has limited incremental practical value.
Realism: postoperative explanation is plausible, but the clinic visit is a wrapper around an anatomy quiz rather than a decision that changes care.
suggestions: Use an independently constructed, labelled operative-orientation exhibit and ask for a concrete repair or structure-protection decision that changes with the observed anatomy.
Compare credible errors in the same operative plane; do not claim resident-level two-step difficulty merely by retaining both vessel and wall labels.

title: Postoperative distension cross-sectional assessment
fairness: CT is a reasonable best choice among the supplied investigations for progressive postoperative abdominal symptoms. There is no clear lexical shortcut; stability and absence of peritoneal findings serve a legitimate triage purpose.
The unspecified operation and interval leave the clinical problem unusually generic. Neither a ductal nor a vascular question is developed to make the alternatives close competitors.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: this is routine broad-imaging selection without interpretation of a prior result or a competing protocol.

Importance: high practical value for postoperative complication assessment. Realism: hospital reassessment from clinic is credible, but a real referral would identify the procedure and postoperative timing.
suggestions: Name the operation and postoperative interval, then give a genuine unresolved finding that distinguishes plausible imaging protocols or a focused study from cross-sectional imaging.
Keep the stability assessment; replace unsupported MRCP/Doppler foils with investigations a resident might actually choose for that specific complication.

title: Postoperative fluid composition

cues.phrase: The hospital has obtained a peritoneal-fluid sample that looks opaque.
cues.why: The newly available sample points directly to the only option that tests peritoneal fluid. Sample-to-test matching works without identifying what opacity means.

cues.phrase: Repeat CT with fluid-attenuation measurement
cues.why: CT has already documented the fluid; without a changed question or protocol limitation, the repeated completed investigation is a disposable foil.

fairness: Fluid triglyceride testing is a defensible response to this presentation. Opacity itself is not proof of chyle, and culture can investigate an alternative explanation.
A CT report without a defined duct injury does not establish absence of every biliary or pancreatic leak; the item should not teach that inference.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: the key uniquely uses the available specimen, while serum lipids and repeat fluid visualization do not answer its composition.
Importance: useful postoperative complication recognition. Realism: clinic review of hospital sampling is plausible, but the task should clarify whether sampling has occurred and results are pending.
suggestions: Compare named peritoneal-fluid assays for plausible competing postoperative leaks, using the operation, fluid course and raw sample findings to distinguish them.
Preserve uncertainty about opacity; remove the implication that unremarkable duct imaging settles the leak mechanism.

title: Nutrition for postoperative chylous leakage

cues.phrase: Liberal long-chain fat with MCT restriction
cues.why: This is the exact directional reversal of the key's two components, spotlighting that pair rather than representing an independently plausible nutrition plan. It narrows guessing but does not by itself identify the key.

cues.phrase: Restricted protein with unchanged long-chain fat
cues.why: The third option changes a different nutrient and is structurally outside the opposing fat/MCT pair, making it easy to discard on test-taking grounds.

fairness: The key is a defensible dietary composition for an initial enteral approach to chylous leakage. The diagnosis is legitimately supplied for a management task.
The task asks what belongs in a recorded plan without actually displaying that plan; it should ask what to prescribe or recommend.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: named chylous ascites followed by the familiar fat modification is single-rule recall. Drainage and monitoring details do not affect selection.

Importance: relevant surgical nutrition, though less broadly encountered than general nutrition-route decisions. Realism: outpatient review of a hospital plan is credible; the present task has no remaining patient-specific choice.
suggestions: Give a supported intake/leak-response record and ask which concrete nutrition adjustment follows, comparing credible regimens at the same treatment stage.
Remove decorative monitoring prose and the reversed-component distractor construction; do not invent output thresholds or challenge durations.

title: Nutrition during prolonged postoperative ileus

cues.phrase: Persistent severe dysfunction; oral and tube feeding both inadequate
cues.why: The exhibit explicitly dismisses both distractor routes, leaving parenteral nutrition by elimination without interpreting patient data.

cues.phrase: No mechanical obstruction or another correctable precipitating diagnosis identified
cues.why: This broad exclusion summary preinterprets the workup and removes the need to consider a reversible explanation; it is not a usable set of reassessment observations.

fairness: Parenteral support is plausible, but inadequate delivery is not synonymous with an unusable gut. Supplemental PN alongside some enteral intake is not represented by the mutually exclusive route labels.
Postoperative day 9 alone does not describe cumulative intake, baseline nutritional risk or anticipated duration. Those details matter more than an isolated day number.
Too easy as written: both wrong answers are declared inadequate. The apparent second step has been performed by the author.
Importance: high-yield perioperative nutrition. Realism: a hospital nutrition record is appropriate, but real route decisions need an intake and tolerance trajectory.
suggestions: Replace 'severe dysfunction' and 'both inadequate' with actual feeding attempts, tolerance and intake relative to assessed needs, plus baseline nutritional status and expected course.
Compare concrete supplemental-PN, enteral-adjustment and continued-observation plans with a clinician-verified timing rationale; do not imply day 9 automatically mandates exclusive PN.

title: Mesh after a controlled enterotomy

cues.phrase: source control was complete
cues.why: This is an authored eligibility conclusion. Together with repeated assurances about repair and spillage, it rehearses the permission to retain a synthetic-mesh strategy. The necessary underlying contamination findings should remain.

fairness: A controlled enterotomy does not by itself make permanent synthetic mesh an indefensible choice. Distinguishing contamination context from material selection can be a meaningful two-step task.
The implant plane, relationship to bowel and fascial closure strategy are absent. A broad material label should not imply identical suitability across all repair configurations.

Biologic mesh is a clinically recognizable competitor, not a universally impossible action. The question should distinguish the preferred plan under specified conditions rather than ask for an unexplained 'supported selection'.

Importance: high practical relevance in abdominal-wall surgery. Realism: operative-record review is plausible, but the record omits important technical context. Exact material-policy claims were not externally verified in this offline review.
suggestions: Specify the intended plane, bowel separation and closure strategy, with concrete operative observations rather than the conclusion 'source control was complete'.
Ask which implant plan is preferred for that defined reconstruction; keep credible materials comparable and have the clinician verify the exact scenario against its evidence.

title: Meckel resection extent

cues.phrase: extending into the adjacent ileum
cues.why: The key is the only option explicitly removing ileum, allowing location-word matching rather than a demanding resection decision.

cues.phrase: the distal tip was relatively preserved
cues.why: This explicitly undermines 'Perform distal diverticular resection', which otherwise adds little credible competition.

fairness: Segmental resection is defensible for disruption involving the base and adjacent bowel. The concern is weak discrimination, not a confidently wrong key.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: removing the named damaged region is the entire decision; the distal-tip distractor leaves the stated disease behind.

Importance: worthwhile emergency small-bowel operative judgment. Realism: the anatomy is plausible, but the task retrospectively asks which operation fit an already completed operation without a meaningful residual question.
suggestions: Compare segmental resection with a genuinely plausible bowel-inclusive wedge approach using observed base geometry, extent and potential luminal compromise.
Use a constructed operative diagram if geometry is decisive; retain the real disease distribution but remove the preserved-tip foil.

title: Celiac serology when IgA is deficient

cues.phrase: Which serologic study
cues.why: The task excludes HLA genotyping by category before any clinical interpretation.

cues.phrase: total IgA is markedly deficient
cues.why: Against an explicitly repeated IgA test and a nonserologic option, this makes the only new antibody class conspicuous. The deficiency is necessary data; the option set creates the shortcut.

cues.phrase: Upper endoscopy has not yet been performed.
cues.why: This named omission adds framing without affecting selection among the offered laboratory choices.

fairness: An appropriate IgG-based celiac assay is defensible in IgA deficiency. 'IgG-based antibody assay panel' is too generic to identify the actual assays being ordered.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: the stem and category mismatch supply almost all the elimination. There is no second consequential decision.
Importance: useful diagnostic-test literacy and malabsorption knowledge, but less central to daily general-surgery decisions than the operative topics in this batch.
Realism: anemia and loose-stool evaluation can reach surgical clinic, although the referral purpose is missing and the next-workup role needs clarification.
suggestions: Name the specific appropriate IgG assays, and compare actual laboratory or endoscopic plans at a common decision stage.
Build a discordant-result or persistent-suspicion decision that requires interpretation before selecting a next step; do not merely hide the essential IgA result.

title: Celiac testing after gluten withdrawal

cues.phrase: he has never had a completed evaluation while eating gluten
cues.why: The named missing evaluation restates the rationale for gluten reintroduction and repeat testing.

cues.phrase: before closing his celiac evaluation
cues.why: The lead-in signals that closing the evaluation is premature, directly disadvantaging the 'End further' option.

cues.phrase: Diagnose celiac disease from the dietary response
cues.why: No dietary response is actually reported, making this a visibly unsupported distractor without needing celiac expertise.

fairness: The prior negatives may be unreliable after gluten withdrawal, but duration and degree of restriction are not supplied. Stopping gluten shortly before testing is not equivalent to prolonged avoidance.

Discussing supervised gluten reintroduction is reasonable; genotype-informed assessment can also be relevant before a challenge. The item should not imply that repeat serology is invariably a complete diagnostic pathway.
Too easy as written: only the key investigates further, while the other options close or diagnose without adequate support.
Importance: useful test-validity principle, of moderate direct relevance to general surgery. Realism: plausible referral review, but the history lacks the exposure timeline a clinician would need.
suggestions: Show the actual diet/testing chronology and ask a neutral next-step question; remove the 'never completed' summary and 'before closing' framing.
Compare concrete, clinician-supported diagnostic sequences, including when susceptibility testing or repeat biopsy is relevant, without inventing challenge doses or durations.

title: Positive celiac susceptibility typing

cues.phrase: The genotype report is the only disease-directed study in her referral packet.
cues.why: This names the missing workup and makes repeating the already supplied genotype a weak foil.

cues.phrase: Total IgA is adequate.
cues.why: The key alone repeats total-IgA language ('with total-IgA interpretation'), while the other antibody option uses IgG. The value is legitimate clinical information, but its option-specific wording amplifies recognition.

fairness: tTG-IgA is a defensible next test with ongoing gluten exposure and adequate IgA. Positive susceptibility typing is not itself a diagnosis.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: repeating a genotype is not a close alternative and the other distractor tests a familiar antibody-class rule. The genotype need not be deeply interpreted to select the key.
Importance: moderate diagnostic literacy value; three closely related celiac items in this batch need a clear distinction in practical learning objectives.
Realism: a referral packet containing susceptibility typing is possible, but why it was obtained before standard testing is unexplained.
suggestions: Remove the key-only interpretive qualifier and name every test consistently.
Use a real discordance between serology, exposure and histology that makes interpretation of susceptibility testing change the next action, rather than simply requesting the missing initial test.

title: HCC tumor burden versus liver resection suitability

cues.phrase: Which referral should be prioritized
cues.why: Only 'Liver-transplant center evaluation' is phrased as a referral; the alternatives are resection scheduling and surveillance.

cues.phrase: Routine hepatic resection scheduling
cues.why: Immediate routine scheduling is an overcommitted alternative to the key's cautious evaluation. The unequal decision stages favor the key independently of transplant criteria.

cues.phrase: combined tumor and liver findings
cues.why: This lead-in tells the learner to seek an option addressing both problems; transplantation is the only option with that conceptual breadth. This is a weaker cue requiring some background knowledge.

fairness: Transplant-center evaluation is defensible for this tumor burden and decompensated cirrhosis; evaluation does not assert eligibility or guarantee transplantation.

Too easy for PGY-2/3 despite an important potential two-step objective: explicit portal hypertension and recurrent ascites are paired with immediate resection or untreated surveillance rather than competing specialist pathways.
Importance: high-yield hepatobiliary oncology. Realism: clinic referral planning is appropriate, but the alternatives do not resemble equally considered multidisciplinary referrals.
suggestions: Ask which treatment-planning pathway to pursue and make all options concrete specialist pathways at the same stage.
Use observed liver-function/decompensation findings and credible competing local treatment or transplant evaluation plans; retain the information needed to avoid inappropriate resection.

title: Structural assessment before gastric emptying

cues.phrase: the sampled tissue was nondiagnostic
cues.why: The summary explicitly names the missing diagnosis; the key is the only option that obtains biopsy tissue.

cues.phrase: before assigning Peter Bell's symptoms to gastroparesis
cues.why: The task announces the sequencing lesson instead of asking neutrally how to investigate the unresolved narrowing.

cues.phrase: High-resolution esophageal manometry
cues.why: The esophageal target does not match the explicitly localized pyloric problem, making this an anatomical outlier rather than a close resident error.

fairness: Further assessment of an untraversed irregular narrowing is appropriate before attributing symptoms to a motility disorder.

The key simply repeats upper endoscopy with biopsy without specifying how the prior sampling limitation will be addressed. Depending on the lesion and prior specimen, cross-sectional imaging or another targeted sampling technique may be important; the visible facts do not establish the optimal repeat protocol.
Too easy as written: the unresolved narrowing and nondiagnostic tissue point to the only tissue-obtaining option. Importance: high-yield obstruction-versus-motility distinction.
Realism: an outpatient referral while tolerating liquids is plausible, but the prior pathology findings, chronology and repeat-procedure plan need detail.
suggestions: Display the actual acquisition and pathology observations explaining why the first specimen could not answer the question.
Ask for the next diagnostic plan and compare plausible structural-assessment strategies, specifying what a repeat procedure would do differently; remove the unrelated esophageal test.

title: Reassessing nutrition after ileus resolves

cues.phrase: meals and between-meal drinks now meet her assessed needs
cues.why: This supplies the interpretation needed to stop primary PN rather than asking the learner to assess an intake record.

cues.phrase: Replace adequate oral intake with tube feeding
cues.why: The distractor labels the route it would replace as adequate, editorially announcing its own lack of indication.

cues.phrase: Her bowel function has returned and she is eating full meals again.
cues.why: This rehearses the oral-transition rationale before the task; the following adequacy sentence repeats the same conclusion.

fairness: Transition away from primary PN is defensible given the stated sustained adequacy. The key's supplements need not be mandatory if ordinary intake already suffices.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: all reasoning about route function and intake adequacy has been completed in the stem.
Importance: high practical nutrition value. Realism: joint surgical/dietitian follow-up is credible, but no real remaining uncertainty distinguishes the plans.
suggestions: Provide a short intake/tolerance trajectory relative to assessed requirements, including a meaningful conflict such as inconsistent intake despite returned bowel function.
Compare concrete oral, supplemental-PN and enteral plans without evaluative words such as 'adequate' inside a wrong option.

title: Incidental gallbladder muscle invasion

cues.phrase: Hepatobiliary surgical consultation
cues.why: This is the only specialist evaluation, competing against routine follow-up or an isolated scar operation. A test-taker can choose escalation for a new cancer without interpreting muscle invasion.

cues.phrase: Port-site scar excision
cues.why: The presentation gives no port-site finding; this is an unsupported anatomical target and a poor alternative to assessment of the documented cancer.

fairness: Hepatobiliary review is a reasonable next plan. The broad referral key avoids asserting that a specific reoperation is appropriate before staging and fitness review.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: changing the depth of invasion may leave 'consult the specialist' as the easiest answer. The critical pathology finding is not made consequential enough.

Importance: high-yield incidental gallbladder cancer management. Realism: the postoperative clinic setting is strong, but the answer lacks the concrete staging or operative decision the owner requests.
suggestions: Supply the staging and fitness information needed to compare concrete management sequences after specialist pathology review.
Use credible plans that differ because of invasion depth and residual-disease assessment, rather than specialist referral versus unsupported scar surgery.

title: Gastric cancer with adjacent-organ invasion

cues.phrase: has not finished assessing overall operative feasibility
cues.why: This names an incomplete assessment, and only the key proposes an assessment rather than a settled operation.

cues.phrase: Gastrectomy with mandatory pancreatic and splenic preservation
cues.why: 'Mandatory' is a conspicuous absolute and preservation of both explicitly invaded organs contradicts the stated distribution.

cues.phrase: Gastrectomy with routine splenectomy and pancreatic preservation
cues.why: 'Routine' advertises an indiscriminate operation, while preserving the explicitly involved pancreas makes elimination straightforward.

cues.phrase: Specialist assessment for en-bloc multivisceral resection
cues.why: The key is uniquely qualified, cautious and broader in scope than the two committed operations.

fairness: Specialist assessment of possible en-bloc resection is defensible, but direct extension alone does not establish resectability or the full multimodality sequence.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: the task is solved by choosing the only unfinished planning step and the only option addressing both invaded structures.
Importance: relevant oncologic operative principle. Realism: multidisciplinary planning is appropriate; the competing plans are caricatures and do not represent the remaining feasibility decision.
suggestions: Compare equally developed treatment-planning sequences and state the actual residual staging or resectability uncertainty.
Remove 'mandatory', 'routine' and the named unfinished-assessment cue. If the target is resection extent, provide feasibility findings and compare concrete operations at that stage.

title: Mammographic mass morphology

cues.phrase: Spiculated
cues.why: Only the keyed row has this margin descriptor; both alternatives repeat 'Circumscribed'. Choosing the unique row is a nonmedical heuristic, although not proof.

cues.phrase: Irregular
cues.why: This ordinary-language abnormality appears only in the key and aligns with the task's 'most concerning' wording.

fairness: Mass B is defensibly most concerning among these descriptions; density does not erase the importance of morphology.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: this is recognition of an archetypal suspicious descriptor, not interpretation followed by a clinical decision.
Importance: breast imaging interpretation is high-yield, but ranking labels adds little beyond basic recognition.
Realism: reviewing radiologist descriptions in clinic is credible. A descriptor table is not an actual mammographic exhibit and should not be presented as an image-reading task.
suggestions: Use a reviewed constructed visual if morphology interpretation is the objective, or a realistic report with a clinical/imaging concordance problem if management is the objective.
Compare plausible next actions and ensure more than one lesion has a concerning component, without making multiple answers equally indicated.

title: Calcification morphology and distribution

cues.phrase: Segmental
cues.why: The keyed group is the sole distribution outlier against two 'Grouped' rows. The learner can select the unique row without understanding calcifications; this is a probabilistic shortcut.

fairness: Fine linear/branching calcifications in a segmental distribution are defensibly the most concerning described pattern.
'Coarse, densely calcified' is less precise than a fully specified morphology; it should not be used to teach that every coarse calcification pattern is benign.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: the table tests one familiar pattern and no consequential next action. Importance: high-yield breast diagnosis, but the current task is foundational recognition.
Realism: radiology-report review is plausible; a morphology task would benefit from an actual usable constructed image rather than only diagnostic vocabulary.
suggestions: Specify each morphology accurately and balance distribution descriptors so the key is not the only unique row.
Add a real sampling or concordance decision that changes with the interpreted findings; do not merely ask for another label for the suspicious group.

title: Palpable breast mass in the thirties

cues.phrase: Diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound
cues.why: This is the only diagnostic, targeted plan and the only combined-modality option for a symptomatic finding.

cues.phrase: with routine recall
cues.why: Both distractors append routine recall to an unresolved persistent mass, making them sound less responsive than the key without requiring knowledge of age-based imaging selection.

fairness: Diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound is reasonable. The item should not imply that this is the only acceptable initial imaging sequence for every woman aged 30–39; targeted ultrasound can also be a legitimate starting investigation depending on context.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: diagnostic versus screening wording does most of the work. Age and pregnancy status do not create a close decision within these options.
Importance: high practical breast-clinic value. Realism: the presentation is realistic, but the MRI and screening plans are not credible peers.
suggestions: Compare legitimate diagnostic pathways rather than screening/recall plans.
Use actual prior imaging and palpable-site concordance to create a meaningful next-step choice, with clinician verification of age-specific appropriateness and no invented cutoff.

title: Benign phyllodes excision planning

cues.phrase: The surgeon can remove the lesion completely with a narrow rim of normal tissue
cues.why: This is the key's operative rationale and repeats 'complete' removal while explicitly making a narrow excision feasible.

cues.phrase: there is no skin or chest-wall involvement
cues.why: With no other stated reason for mastectomy, this further weakens the already extreme mastectomy distractor. The finding may be legitimate eligibility information in a better option set.

fairness: The alternatives overlap: 'Perform excision with 10-mm margins' is also a complete excision. The generic key does not exclude the second option, and the task does not ask for the least necessary extent. A unique answer is not adequately defined.
A wider complete excision is not automatically an incorrect operation merely because that width is not required. The item conflates a minimum requirement with an impermissible alternative.

Too easy superficially, but the option overlap is unfair rather than useful difficulty. Importance: avoiding unnecessary breast-tissue removal is practical; the exact current benign-phyllodes recommendation needs clinician verification.
Realism: preoperative clinic planning is appropriate, but the presentation has already selected the limited procedure.
suggestions: Rebuild mutually exclusive plans with explicit intended margins and a concrete patient-specific consequence of the wider operation.

Ask which extent is recommended under a verified benign-phyllodes policy, rather than which operation is generically complete; remove the preannounced feasibility rationale while retaining necessary lesion/breast anatomy.

title: Benign phyllodes margin after excision
fairness: Surveillance is defensible for the narrowly described intact benign-phyllodes excision without suspected residual tumor; wider re-excision is a credible competing resident response to tumor at ink.

The no-transection and residual-mass findings are decision-critical, not disposable negatives: tumor touching ink is not necessarily equivalent to a transected lesion with residual disease. They should not be deleted merely to increase difficulty.

Meaningful two-step reasoning: interpret the positive margin in the operative/specimen context, then choose management according to benign histology. No strong nonmedical key-selection cue or length outlier was found.
Importance: useful breast-surgery decision preventing reflex reoperation. Realism: a postoperative pathology visit with operative correlation is appropriate.

Editorial PASS only. Exact contemporary surveillance/re-excision guidance has not been independently source-verified in this no-network review, and this does not confer Melissa Rowland's clinical approval.
suggestions: Preserve the grade, intact-specimen and residual-disease observations through subsequent revisions. Have the named clinician confirm the exact policy and follow-up wording before clinical approval.
Do not expose feedback from a preceding benign-phyllodes item that states this management answer before this question is attempted.

title: Borderline phyllodes close-margin action

cues.phrase: The excision bed is small relative to the remaining breast, with no skin or chest-wall involvement.
cues.why: This packages the feasibility rationale for limited re-excision and specifically undermines completion mastectomy. It narrows the options without requiring knowledge of the margin recommendation.

fairness: Re-excision at a 2-mm borderline-phyllodes margin may match a particular guideline, but that guideline is not identified in the visible task. Negative-margin width recommendations are policy-sensitive; I cannot establish that surveillance is universally indefensible from these fields alone.
Difficulty is moderate because the exact recommendation is specialized, not because the item demands two-step reasoning. The generic feasibility sentence does not create a genuine second decision.
Importance: margin management is useful in breast surgery; memorizing one exact recommendation is narrower than the general clinical principle and its ABSITE relevance is not verified here.
Realism: postoperative clinic is appropriate, but grade, margin and breast size alone may not resolve individualized reoperation decisions under all accepted policies.
suggestions: State the verified guideline/version being applied or give the applicable policy as an exhibit and test its use in a clinically meaningful case.

Describe actual cavity anatomy and additional margin/pathology features when they change the choice; compare credible re-excision and observation plans without a straw-man mastectomy. Obtain clinician adjudication of the surveillance distractor.

title: Malignant phyllodes close-margin action

cues.phrase: The excision bed is small relative to the remaining breast, with no skin or chest-wall involvement.
cues.why: As in the borderline item, this is an explicit breast-conservation feasibility rationale that removes the mastectomy distractor. Repeated wording also creates a batch-level pattern for selecting re-excision.

fairness: Re-excision for this 4-mm malignant-phyllodes margin may be the intended recommendation, but the visible question does not specify the guideline or patient-specific considerations supporting a universal ranking over surveillance.
I am not asserting that the key is clinically wrong; the exact margin policy requires source and clinician adjudication, unavailable under this review's constraints.
Moderate predicted difficulty reflects specialized margin recall. Grade plus a number followed by the matching intervention is not automatically two-step reasoning.
Importance: practically relevant breast oncology, but this is close duplication of the borderline-margin item unless the changed histology meaningfully changes a decision.
Realism: the clinic scenario is credible; the generic conservation-permission sentence and omission of a defined policy make it less representative of actual multidisciplinary planning.
suggestions: Identify the applicable verified recommendation and make the task explicit about the local margin decision, without pretending this settles all adjuvant management.
Use a case where the margin location or operative consequence creates a real competing plan; have the clinician confirm that the offered alternatives rank uniquely.

title: Axillary surgery in phyllodes
fairness: Omitting routine axillary surgery is defensible for the described phyllodes case. Sentinel-node biopsy is a credible misconception transferred from epithelial breast cancer.
The unremarkable axilla is necessary context; it is not by itself an unfair cue, since node-negative epithelial breast cancer can still require staging. No strong purely lexical shortcut was found.
Too easy for typical PGY-2/3 residents familiar with the phyllodes rule: the diagnosis is given and the only task is recalling whether routine axillary staging is done.
Importance: high practical value in avoiding an unnecessary operation. Realism: planning the axillary component of a mastectomy is a good clinic task.
suggestions: Keep the clinically important objective but require interpretation of a realistic histology or node-evaluation discrepancy before selecting the axillary plan.
Alternatively seek explicit acceptance as a foundational recognition item; do not describe the unchanged version as two-step resident difficulty.

title: A suspicious node in phyllodes

cues.phrase: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy
cues.why: The key alone samples the actual abnormal node before committing to a staging or clearance operation. The option-stage mismatch makes a generic 'diagnose first' heuristic sufficient.

fairness: Targeted tissue evaluation is reasonable for a new abnormal node; phyllodes biology should not justify ignoring an unexplained enlarging node.

The presentation does not show sonographic characterization or prior sampling. This does not make a planned ultrasound-guided biopsy wrong, but it leaves little specific clinical reasoning to perform.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: two immediate operative alternatives are weak before establishing what the node represents.
Importance: useful avoidance of both dismissal and overtreatment. Realism: a new node at follow-up is credible, but a real next-step plan would incorporate targeted imaging findings.
suggestions: Provide observed ultrasound features and any relevant prior tissue result, then compare plausible diagnostic or surveillance plans at the same stage.
Make the error tested failure to reconcile the node with the tumor biology, rather than merely choosing needle biopsy over axillary dissection.

title: Borderline phyllodes operative margin target
fairness: Naming the UK Association of Breast Surgery appropriately limits the policy being tested, but 'recorded' implies a record that is not shown. The guideline version is unspecified and its exact number has not been verified in this offline review.
No robust nonmedical cue selects 5 mm from the otherwise parallel plans; a middle-value guess is not sufficient evidence of a specific cue.
Moderate difficulty is specialized number recall. The table simply encodes three widths and adds no interpretation or second clinical decision.

Importance: grade-specific margin planning has value, but memorizing one organization's exact target has lower incremental general-surgery value than applying it to a real resection tradeoff. ABSITE scope is not established by naming a guideline.
Realism: the artificial equivalence of all reconstructions removes the patient considerations that normally make a surgical plan consequential.
suggestions: Merge this objective into a margin-management case or provide the verified policy/version as a reference exhibit and test application to actual specimen anatomy.
Do not manufacture difficulty through an unexplained exact number; make the outcome of choosing a different margin clinically meaningful.

title: Malignant phyllodes operative margin target
fairness: The named UK policy narrows the intended answer, but the edition and supposed recorded recommendation are absent. This review has not independently verified the exact 10-mm claim.
No decisive lexical or length cue was found. 'Malignant means widest' is a generic clinical heuristic, not proof that the numeric recommendation is understood.
Moderate difficulty reflects recall of a guideline number; reading a one-column width table is not an additional reasoning step.
Importance: useful local-control principle, but low incremental value alongside the malignant close-margin question unless it tests a distinct practical decision.
Realism: making every option equally conserving with identical reconstruction eliminates the operative tradeoff and makes the clinic setting decorative.
suggestions: Combine with a specimen-margin or re-excision problem that requires choosing a concrete operation under a specified, verified policy.
If retained separately, show actual anatomic/reconstructive consequences and avoid treating a guideline target as a universal adequacy threshold for every negative margin.

title: Phyllodes dissemination pattern

cues.phrase: confirmed distant disease despite an unremarkable axilla
cues.why: The lead-in restates both facts specifically to eliminate contiguous and regional-lymphatic options, leaving the remaining route. It teaches the contrast the learner should infer.

cues.phrase: Direct contiguous extension
cues.why: Ordinary spatial meaning conflicts with the explicitly distant lung lesion, making this a nonfunctioning alternative.

fairness: Hematogenous dissemination is the defensible expected pattern for the described stromal tumor. Normal axillary imaging alone does not prove the actual route of an individual metastasis.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: the task requests a route label after metastatic origin has already been supplied; there is no management inference.
Importance: relevant underlying tumor biology, but lower practical value than the related axillary-management decisions already represented in this batch.
Realism: reviewing metastatic pathology in clinic is plausible, but the encounter calls for a treatment/staging plan rather than naming a route.
suggestions: Merge the biological objective into a concrete staging, biopsy or operative decision so understanding spread changes care.
Avoid implying that an unremarkable axilla proves the route; remove the repeated contrast from the task.

title: Overt renin-independent aldosterone production
fairness: The combination of spontaneous hypokalemia, suppressed renin and elevated aldosterone supports the intended overt phenotype. CT plus AVS is a defensible pathway for a 51-year-old seeking surgical treatment if unilateral disease is demonstrated.

Two meaningful errors compete: unnecessary suppression testing in an overt phenotype and choosing surgery from CT laterality alone. The learner must interpret the biochemical context and then select the subtype-assessment pathway.

The surgery preference is decision-critical rather than gratuitous permission: it changes the value of pursuing laterality. Corrected potassium and managed medication interference establish test context; detailed drug troubleshooting is not the task being scored.
No compelling nonmedical wording, convergence or option-length cue was found. All alternatives include CT and differ in consequential sequencing.
Importance: high-yield endocrine-surgery workup. Realism: outpatient referral planning is appropriate; the combined key should be read as a pathway, not a demand for simultaneous procedures.

Editorial PASS only; assay-specific criteria and contemporary guideline applicability still require exact-version clinical/source confirmation. No external verification or clinical sign-off occurred in this review.
suggestions: Preserve assay identification, the biochemical values and the surgical-intent context. Confirm the exact exception to suppression testing and AVS pathway with the named clinician.
Keep any explanation of the diagnostic threshold and CT-versus-AVS distinction after the answer.

title: Factor assessment after an inhibitory mixing pattern

cues.phrase: Repeat immediate mixing with procedural clearance
cues.why: This distractor advertises that it will ignore the later abnormal result and grant clearance. It combines a test with an unjustified consequence while the key simply investigates.

cues.phrase: Inherited bleeding-disorder genotyping first
cues.why: 'First' flags a sequencing error, and the option is a broad genetic category rather than a focused laboratory plan comparable with the key.

cues.phrase: Specimen problems and anticoagulant interference have been assessed by the laboratory.
cues.why: This reassuring process summary invites the reader to treat confounding as excluded without reporting what the assessment found.

fairness: New bruising and delayed loss of mixing correction support investigating a time-dependent inhibitor, making factor VIII activity and inhibitor testing defensible.
'Assessed' does not actually say interference was absent or resolved. The intended clean interpretation needs the relevant laboratory conclusion or observations.
There is a genuine mechanism-to-testing inference, of moderate expected difficulty, but weak alternatives let a learner bypass it.

Importance: high practical perioperative bleeding assessment. Realism: hematology review before elective surgery is appropriate; the plain-language mixing narrative could be a usable immediate/incubated-results exhibit.
suggestions: Show immediate and incubated results with the actual relevant interference assessment, then compare similarly specific laboratory panels.
Remove procedural clearance and the 'first' qualifier from distractors; use plausible alternative inhibitor or factor-assessment pathways, with clinician-confirmed ranking.

title: New swelling despite established lymphedema

cues.phrase: Routine pelvic staging CT
cues.why: 'Routine' contrasts with an acute postoperative change and makes this sound like a delayed background task rather than an investigation of the present problem.

fairness: Venous duplex is a defensible first investigation of newly worsened tender postoperative leg swelling. The stable status is useful context, not a cue to remove.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: standard postoperative DVT recognition defeats arterial imaging and routine staging without requiring meaningful reinterpretation of the lymphedema history.

Importance: high practical value in preventing anchoring on chronic edema. Realism: the new symptoms warrant prompt assessment in a surgical follow-up setting; the task should state the urgency rather than frame it as routine compression adjustment.
suggestions: Keep the safety-critical symptom change; if a deliberately easy safety item is desired, request explicit acceptance of that purpose.

For resident-level reasoning, use a prior venous study with specified coverage/adequacy and a persistent proximal concern, then compare credible next investigations. Do not add an unsupported imaging threshold.

title: Symptom control versus thyroid-hormone production

cues.phrase: reduces thyroid-hormone production rather than mainly explaining Caroline Ward's improved palpitations
cues.why: The task supplies the mechanism-versus-symptom distinction and explicitly distances the answer from the beta-blocker already linked to the improved palpitations.

cues.phrase: Thionamide antithyroid therapy
cues.why: 'Antithyroid' semantically matches reducing thyroid production, whereas 'Thyroid-hormone replacement therapy' contradicts the described hormone excess even to a reader using ordinary word meanings.

cues.phrase: Her endocrine team is reviewing disease-directed therapy
cues.why: This previews the intended drug category instead of adding a patient constraint that distinguishes real treatments.

fairness: Thionamides are the defensible class among these choices. The beta-blocker distinction is appropriate at the broad level asked, but the item should avoid teaching that beta-blockers have no other thyroid-related effects in any circumstance.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: this is basic drug-class matching, not interpretation followed by a treatment choice.
Importance: high practical perioperative endocrine management, currently assessed below the intended resident level.
Realism: preoperative endocrine optimization is plausible, but the owner requests actual medicines or treatment plans rather than generic classes.
suggestions: Ask a neutral concrete treatment question and name actual medicines in every option.
Give a supported patient-specific treatment constraint or trajectory that makes two credible disease-directed plans compete; keep the production-versus-symptom explanation in feedback.

title: IVC filter versus anticoagulation for a provoked DVT

cues.phrase: no active bleeding or other contraindication to anticoagulant treatment
cues.why: This explicitly grants permission for the keyed treatment and removes the principal reason to consider the filter option, instead of showing the relevant postoperative bleeding observations.

cues.phrase: no limb-threatening venous findings
cues.why: This second broad negative maps directly onto the aggressive-intervention distractor. It is necessary safety context in principle, but the paired exclusion summaries pre-solve this option set.

cues.phrase: uncomplicated provoked DVT
cues.why: The task adds an interpretive reassurance label after the stem has already eliminated the special-case alternatives.

fairness: Therapeutic anticoagulation is defensible under the stated conditions. The problem is not that necessary bleeding or limb-threat information should be hidden.

Too easy for PGY-2/3: the diagnosis is supplied and the alternative indications are explicitly excluded. Resolution of the provoking factor does not materially change the initial choice among these options.
Importance: high-yield postoperative VTE treatment. Realism: the operation, elapsed time and actual hemostatic status are missing from a situation where clinicians would examine them.
suggestions: Replace generic eligibility summaries with actual postoperative bleeding and limb observations and ask a neutral treatment question.
Compare credible anticoagulation/filter sequences in a case with a real, well-supported temporary constraint; do not create ambiguity by simply deleting safety data.

title: Investigating oxygen-carrying capacity

cues.phrase: His discharge packet contains no postoperative laboratory results.
cues.why: This names the missing action, and the complete blood count is the only offered laboratory test.

cues.phrase: saturation within its reference range with a good signal
cues.why: The immediately available apparently adequate oximetry makes repeating it a conspicuously weak option without any changed indication or signal problem.

cues.phrase: substantial hemorrhage
cues.why: Ordinary blood-loss-to-blood-count matching points to the key; the two alternatives concern respiratory monitoring rather than a plausible competing cause of the fatigue.

fairness: A CBC is reasonable after hemorrhage with fatigue and no postoperative hemoglobin record. Normal saturation does not establish normal oxygen-carrying capacity.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: the investigation follows directly from blood loss, and the missing-laboratory sentence does the remaining selection work.
Importance: fundamental and clinically important, but this version is closer to foundational physiology than resident application.

Realism: postoperative fatigue is plausible; a substantial inpatient hemorrhage without available postoperative labs should prompt attention to record retrieval and bleeding status, not just a generic test menu.
suggestions: Use an actual hemoglobin/saturation trajectory and ask a consequential, clinician-supported assessment or treatment decision that requires distinguishing saturation from oxygen content.
Remove the named missing laboratory record as a key cue and offer comparable diagnostic plans. Do not invent a transfusion threshold to force difficulty.

title: Tissue sampling after inadequate neck FNA

cues.phrase: A third identical fine-needle aspiration
cues.why: 'Third identical' openly labels the option as repetition of an already unsuccessful procedure rather than a credible optimized sampling plan.

cues.phrase: could not classify the process or complete the required ancillary studies
cues.why: This legitimate specimen limitation points to greater tissue acquisition; paired with an explicitly identical repeat and an open incision, it makes the core option the conspicuous intermediate choice.

fairness: Image-guided core biopsy is defensible to obtain additional tissue after these FNAs, and recognizing the material limitation before changing technique can be meaningful two-step reasoning.

The appropriate architecture-preserving sampling route depends on suspected lymphoid disease, node accessibility, pathology needs and local expertise. Excisional biopsy may be a credible competitor; it should not be silently represented by the less well-defined 'open incisional biopsy'.
The broad task 'consider' can encompass more than one reasonable approach. The supplied facts do not prove that core is uniquely preferable in every suspected lymphoid process.

Importance: high practical value in neck-node diagnosis and tissue stewardship. Realism: solid-target documentation is useful, but the repeat sampling strategy should be tied to the pathologist's concrete material requirements.
suggestions: State the actual missing tissue/ancillary requirement and node accessibility, then ask for the preferred next approach under those conditions.
Compare core with a genuine optimized FNA or excisional-biopsy strategy; remove 'third identical' and have a clinician adjudicate the closest surgical-biopsy alternative.

title: Perioperative respiratory acid-base trajectory

cues.phrase: Respiratory acidosis from retained carbon dioxide
cues.why: The key alone repeats the exhibit's uniquely increasing analyte, arterial CO2, in expanded words. Its causal explanation gives a direct matching route.

cues.phrase: Metabolic alkalosis following gastric acid losses
cues.why: The option introduces gastric losses not present in the record and names alkalosis despite the explicitly falling pH; it is not a close alternative.

fairness: The displayed trend is compatible with acute respiratory acidosis. Relative directions without absolute values do not establish severity, compensation or exclusion of a mixed disorder; the item should not imply more than the table supports.

'Retained' CO2 may be read as a specific hypoventilation mechanism, although a laparoscopic CO2 load can contribute. The data identify a respiratory acid-base direction more securely than a single mechanism.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: higher CO2 and lower pH is basic pattern recognition. No management decision follows.
Importance: high-yield perioperative physiology. Realism: reviewing an anesthetic event is plausible, but the adjective-only table replaces the actual gas and ventilatory context.
suggestions: Provide internally consistent, clinician-verified gas values and ventilatory observations, then ask for a concrete response that depends on distinguishing competing causes or mixed processes.
Use parallel options without causal explanations that merely restate a table cell; do not fabricate compensation cutoffs.

title: Reassessing a changing hand burn

cues.phrase: Arrange specialist burn-center consultation
cues.why: The key is the only cautious specialist assessment between simply continuing care and committing to excision/grafting. The unequal stages favor referral without precisely interpreting burn depth.

cues.phrase: changed burn examination
cues.why: The task highlights deterioration as the trigger for escalation instead of requiring the learner to decide what the individual findings imply.

fairness: Burn-specialist consultation is defensible for a potentially deepening hand burn. The current observations are useful and should not be erased to create difficulty.

The hand location and initial injury may already justify specialist input; the answer can remain the same if the entire changed examination is removed. The before/after comparison therefore may not earn a second inference.
Too easy for PGY-2/3 as a routine difficulty item, though important as a safety-recognition item. Excision/grafting is not established by these descriptions alone.
Importance: high practical importance because hand function matters. Realism: reassessment is credible, but the interval, prior specialist involvement and local burn-care capability are unstated.
suggestions: Clarify prior burn-center involvement and the actual remaining decision; keep the raw examination changes and necessary safety findings.
Compare plans at the same stage that change with the reassessment, or obtain explicit acceptance as an intentionally easy safety/referral item.

title: Paired treatments for urgent VKA reversal
fairness: Intravenous vitamin K is the defensible adjunct to rapid factor replacement in the described emergency warfarin reversal. The option route and drug-name style are parallel, with no strong nonmedical cue.

Too easy for PGY-2/3: the anticoagulant and PCC component are supplied, leaving one familiar antidote-pairing rule. Protamine and idarucizumab are antidotes for different anticoagulants, not close alternatives once warfarin is explicit.

Importance: high-yield and potentially safety-critical. Realism: a postoperative medication review is plausible, but the patient asking about a hospital record supplies no applied decision beyond recall.
suggestions: Use a concrete reversal/reassessment record with a clinically meaningful sequencing or durability problem, and compare plausible complete regimens rather than unrelated anticoagulant antidotes.
Preserve any verified emergency treatment facts and obtain explicit basic/safety-item acceptance if retaining simple drug matching. Do not add invented doses or redosing intervals.

title: Rapid VKA factor replacement
fairness: Four-factor PCC is the defensible preferred product among these choices for rapid reversal in major warfarin-associated bleeding. There is no convincing lexical or option-length giveaway; the two PCC labels are genuinely parallel.
Too easy for typical PGY-2/3 residents: this is preferred-product recall after the clinical problem and treatment component have been named. The clinic wrapper adds no interpretation.

Importance: high-yield emergency hemostasis. Realism: retrospective explanation is possible, but the task does not reproduce the actual decision about urgency, product availability or the patient's response.

Sequence limitation: the separate vitamin-K item explicitly names four-factor PCC in its presentation. If visible before this item in the same learning sequence, it rehearses this answer; runtime ordering was not inspected under the visible-field-only scope.
suggestions: Test a distinct, clinician-supported management decision using an actual anticoagulant/reversal trajectory rather than asking for the product name already supplied by the sibling item.
If kept as a foundational item, seek explicit acceptance of that purpose and ensure preceding visible content does not supply its answer.

title: Early nutrition after an extensive burn

cues.phrase: Recorded oral intake was negligible.
cues.why: This directly defeats the oral-primary-route distractor, leaving little intake interpretation.

cues.phrase: resuscitation was adequate
cues.why: An authored readiness conclusion replaces the physiologic observations needed to judge whether early feeding is appropriate.

cues.phrase: no intestinal ischemia or mechanical obstruction
cues.why: This explicitly removes the gut contraindications relevant to the PN competitor, completing an option-by-option elimination alongside negligible oral intake. Preserve genuinely necessary safety information in a less preinterpreted case.

fairness: Early enteral feeding is defensible for the intended resuscitated extensive-burn patient with inadequate oral intake and a usable gastrointestinal tract.

The exact 'within 24 hours' timing has not been source-verified here. Hemodynamic/support trajectory and burn extent are summarized rather than shown; do not imply feeding irrespective of ongoing resuscitation instability.
Too easy for PGY-2/3: the stem establishes the familiar 'cannot eat, gut usable' rule and excludes both other routes.
Importance: high-yield burn and critical-care nutrition. Realism: hospital-record review is credible, but 'adequate' is not a usable ICU physiology record.
suggestions: Show the actual resuscitation/support and intake trajectory, and compare concrete nutrition-initiation plans that remain plausible until those data are interpreted.
Verify the exact timing claim and retain safety-critical gut/perfusion observations; do not increase difficulty by hiding contraindications or inventing a vasopressor threshold.

title: Planned thoracic injury exposure

cues.phrase: he did not require resuscitative chest access
cues.why: This repeats the distinguishing word in 'Left anterolateral resuscitative thoracotomy' and explicitly eliminates that option.

cues.phrase: planned repair
cues.why: Together with the repeated stability/planning statements, the lead-in reinforces elimination of the sole resuscitative option rather than adding a second decision.

fairness: Right posterolateral exposure is defensible for a middle intrathoracic esophageal injury with associated azygos injury. The side-specific anatomy supplies the actual clinical discriminator.
Moderate expected difficulty comes from thoracic operative anatomy, not from two independent inferences; the access-versus-resuscitation distinction is already answered in the stem.
Importance: worthwhile trauma/foregut exposure knowledge for general-surgery residents, although less frequently encountered than common clinic decisions.

Realism: reviewing a completed thoracic repair is plausible, but the clinic framing is a wrapper around operative-access recall. A labelled constructed localization exhibit would make the anatomical task more meaningful.
suggestions: Keep the physiology needed to establish the operative setting once, and remove the explicit resuscitative-access exclusion and repeated planning language.
Compare credible planned exposures with a constructed injury-localization exhibit; make both injury level and associated structure necessary to choose the approach.
